analysis.one_liner: Caps spending by House candidates at $500,000 per election cycle.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have capped House campaign spending at $500,000 per cycle, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend campaign finance law to limit how much a candidate for the House of Representatives can spend on their own election: $500,000 total per cycle, split evenly between the primary and general election, with an extra $250,000 allowed for runoffs. The limits would rise with inflation, and candidates who exceed them would pay escalating civil penalties to the Federal Election Commission. Spending on campaign legal services would be excluded from the cap. The stated goal is to reduce the endless fundraising Members do and make running for office realistic for more Americans.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be would-be candidates who cannot raise large sums, since a fixed spending cap shrinks the advantage of the best-funded campaigns, and voters who want elections decided less by money. Members of Congress would also spend less time fundraising. Whether competitive elections would actually become more common is uncertain, since outside groups' spending was not addressed.

how_it_helps.text: It would cap a House candidate's total campaign expenditures at $500,000 per election cycle, with no more than $250,000 per primary and $250,000 per general election.
It would allow an additional $250,000 in spending for runoff elections and would index the limits to inflation, with a 2018 base year.
It would impose escalating civil penalties on candidates who exceed the limits: matching the excess below 2.5% of the cap, tripling the excess above that, plus additional FEC penalties above 5%.
The bill's findings argue that unlimited spending harms public confidence in elections and that limiting fundraising would make lawmakers more accountable to constituents.

analysis.who_pays: Candidates who currently spend far more than $500,000 to run — especially in expensive media markets — would have to run on much less. Big-dollar donors lose some influence, and the campaign industry that converts large budgets into consulting, ads, and legal work would see the demand for those services shrink. Whether the cap would help incumbents or challengers more depends on the race.

drawbacks.text: The Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo decision struck down mandatory limits on campaign spending as unconstitutional under the First Amendment; the bill's own findings acknowledge the Court 'failed to recognize' the problem, meaning the cap would almost certainly require a change in that precedent to survive a legal challenge.

The bill excludes campaign legal services from the cap entirely, so a candidate could spend unlimited amounts on lawyers, a carve-out that weakens the limit and favors those with access to campaign counsel.

A hard spending cap can cut both ways: it limits a well-funded challenger's ability to build name recognition against an established incumbent, and it does nothing about outside groups, which can spend without limit — so the bill could entrench incumbents while leaving the biggest money untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea has real appeal: capping spending could reduce the fundraising treadmill for members and open the door to candidates without wealthy networks. But the bill was poorly matched to the legal reality — direct spending limits were ruled unconstitutional in Buckley v. Valeo decades ago, and this bill does nothing about independent expenditures, which now dominate expensive races. The unlimited legal-services carve-out further undercuts its own cap. As designed, it was more a statement of principle than an enforceable reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Higgins introduced the bill on March 19, 2015.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which handles election law.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system stayed exactly as it was: unlimited candidate spending, heavy reliance on big donors, and a permanent campaign fundraising culture. Incumbents and the campaign-consulting and legal industries that feed on large campaign budgets were better off than they would have been under the cap. Even supporters gained little, since the bill never advanced and would have faced a constitutional obstacle anyway.

for.name: Rep. Brian Higgins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap House campaign spending at $500,000 per cycle and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral for election law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan voting pattern ever formed; it simply never moved.

industries.industry: Campaign consulting, advertising, and media firms
industries.note: A $500,000 cap would sharply shrink the pool of campaign money available for consultants, polling, and media buys in House races. Their interest in unlimited client spending does not align with voters' interest in lower-cost elections, though the bill's failure left them unaffected.

The bill explicitly excludes legal services from the spending cap, so even under a $500,000 limit a campaign could spend unlimited amounts on lawyers. This carve-out makes legal counsel the one campaign expense with no ceiling.

industries.industry: Large donors and wealthy self-funding candidates
industries.note: Capping candidate expenditures would reduce the weight of money in House races, though the bill leaves independent group spending untouched.
